h: Village walks, hills and a bit of Outlander
p: Plan on two or three hours for the palace and gardens, then leave time for the village itself, because Falkland is the kind of place you don't want to leave in a hurry. Its old streets of stone houses and pantiled roofs are so well preserved that it became Scotland's first conservation area back in 1970, and you can feel that care as you wander about.

Outlander fans, take note. Falkland stood in for 1940s Inverness in the TV series, and the Bruce Fountain on the main street is one of the spots people come to see. Even if you've never watched an episode, the square, the old inns and the little lanes behind them make for a lovely potter, with tearooms and cafés to duck into when the legs need a rest.

Then there are the hills. The Lomonds rise right behind the village, and East Lomond is a popular climb with sweeping views across Fife on a clear day. The wider Falkland Estate has woodland walks too, so there's something for every level of energy, from a gentle stroll to a proper leg-stretcher. Wear sturdy shoes and take a layer, because it's breezier up top than down in the square.

Falkland makes an easy add-on to a wider Fife trip. St Andrews, with its beaches, cathedral ruins and famous golf links, is within a comfortable drive to the east. Head west instead and you'll reach Kinross and Loch Leven, where Mary, Queen of Scots was once imprisoned on an island castle. The same queen who loved Falkland's hunting and fresh air, which is a nice bit of symmetry for your day out.
